(Today through Saturday)...
Issued at 231 AM EDT Sun Aug 9 2026

THIS MORNING THROUGH TONIGHT...

A continued very humid airmass beneath a shallow but extremely stout 
nocturnal inversion this morning should allow for the development of 
areas of fog across much of the area, with patchy dense fog 
possible. Any fog that develops will mix out quickly in typical 
diurnal fashion in the hour or so after sunrise.

Much of today is likely to be quiet, though an isolated shower or 
storm cannot be completely ruled out. Modest destabilization will 
occur this afternoon, but a moderately strong cap centered at or 
just above 800 mb and a lack of significant forcing for ascent 
should keep a lid on precip until late in the day at the earliest.

Convection is likely to develop this morning along the nose of a 
modest low level jet over the upper Midwest, and then propagating 
ESE along with the aforementioned jet and a slowly retreating 
surface boundary over the lower Great Lakes. This convective system 
will likely serve as the focus for a potential severe threat late 
today into tonight, particularly across the northern half or so of 
Indiana. Intensification of this system is likely as it moves into a 
diurnally destabilizing airmass through the day, and additional 
development is likely along its southern flank as the cold pool 
encounters the aforementioned instability, which may be substantial. 
Sufficient deep layer shear will be present to support storm 
organization, with damaging winds the primary threat, though some 
modest veering may also support a low tornado threat.

Additionally, heavy rain and localized flooding will continue to be 
a threat owing to a seasonably moist airmass and efficient rain 
rates thanks to seasonably high freezing levels and deep warm rain 
processes, on ground that, in spots, has received substantial rain 
in the past week or so.

The window for a severe threat is broad owing to uncertainties 
regarding exact storm evolution, but should encompass the evening 
hours and into the overnight tonight.

Highs today will again rise into the upper 80s and low 90s across 
the area, particularly as little relief from convection is expected 
until late in the day at the earliest. As a result, heat index 
values will peak in the mid 90s to around 100 degrees, producing at 
least a low heat stress threat, particularly for vulnerable 
populations. Continued high humidity will limit lows to the low to 
mid 70s tonight, offering little respite from the heat.

MONDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY NIGHT...

Heat and humidity, along with multiple rounds of possibly severe 
storms, will remain a concern through Wednesday night. While the 
general pattern of ridge-riding convection is apparent and fairly 
seasonally classic, so is the presence of high and growing 
uncertainty with each passing episode of convection, as the prior 
episodes and their shifting outflows, MCVs, etc., will influence the 
development of subsequent rounds of storms, and predictability of 
these features is modest at best, particularly with time.

It appears that the aforementioned boundary, which will meander 
across areas north of the region until it moves into the area mid 
week, along with subtle upper level disturbances and broad forcing 
for ascent from the jet will combine with the heat and humidity 
south of the boundary to spark renewed convection somewhere north or 
northwest of the area Monday afternoon which will then ESE into the 
strong instability through the evening hours. Again, damaging winds 
and heavy rain/flooding will be the primary threats, but an isolated 
tornado cannot be ruled out.

This scenario appears likely to repeat Tuesday, with renewed 
convective development occurring near or upstream and pushing into 
the area during the afternoon and into the overnight, and again on 
Wednesday, though the origin of the convection will likely be closer 
each day as the effective surface boundary sags into the region and 
is reinforced by prior convective cold pools.

The WPC excessive rainfall contains all or part of central Indiana 
through day 5, which is quite reasonable given the aforementioned 
factors supporting heavy rainfall and the potential for multiple 
rounds of significant rainfall. HREF local probability matched means 
through only 00Z Tuesday show peak rainfall totals to our north as 
high as 4-7 inches, demonstrating the capacity for organized 
convection to produce very heavy rainfall, and the background 
setting for heavy rain will not change significantly through 
Wednesday night.

Heat will continue to be a concern for all or part of the area 
through at least Tuesday and perhaps into Wednesday, depending upon 
storm and cloud coverage, with afternoon heat indices as high as the 
low to mid 100s, especially Monday.

THURSDAY ONWARD...
